analogies.phrase: a recipe you follow, or a taste you picked up
analogies.explain: A rule is a recipe. Someone wrote every step. Learning is a taste you picked up. Nobody wrote it down. You just saw enough to know.
A machine only knows what it has seen. Its photo album is the whole world to it.

analogies.phrase: an album shot in only one room
analogies.explain: If every photo was taken in one room, the machine thinks the world is that room.

analogies.phrase: the bricks that words are built from
analogies.explain: A machine does not read words. It reads small bricks. Some bricks are whole words. Some are only part of one.

analogies.phrase: a map where meaning is distance
analogies.explain: Words that mean the same thing sit close together. Words that do not sit far apart.
Each dial makes one thing count more or less. Learning means turning dials until the answer sounds right.
You cannot see the bottom. You can feel which way is down. So you take one small step that way, again and again.

analogies.phrase: the friend who never says I do not know
analogies.explain: Some people answer every question, even when they have no idea. They sound just as sure when they are wrong.

analogies.phrase: a recipe with a helper who can go and fetch things
analogies.explain: On its own a model can only talk. Give it a helper who can look things up, and it can act.

lessons.title: Ask like you mean it
lessons.goal: Write a prompt that names who it is for, the job, the limits, and the shape of the answer.
lessons.intro: Here is the most useful thing you will learn all year, and you get it first. Talking to an AI is a real skill, not magic words. The trick is simple: if you are vague, you get a vague answer back. Let us make yours sharp, right now.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Write me something about dogs.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Here are nine hundred words on the history of dogs. In Latin.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: That is not what I wanted at all!

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: You did not say what you wanted. So I guessed. I am a champion guesser.

lessons.play_brief: Write a prompt in the box. A little checklist lights up as you cover each of the four parts: who it is for, the job, the limits, and the shape. Try to light up all four.

teach.heading: Vague in, vague out
teach.body: "Write about dogs" could mean a poem, a list, a school report, or a joke. The AI cannot read your mind, so it picks one — and it is usually not the one you meant. This is not the AI being dim. It is you not saying enough.

teach.heading: The four parts of a good ask
teach.body: A strong prompt names four things. Who it is for — a six-year-old needs different words than your teacher. The job — explain, list, compare, write. The limits — how long, what to leave out. The shape — a list, a table, three sentences. Name those four and the answer changes completely.

teach.heading: You are giving instructions, not making a wish
teach.body: Think of it like sending a friend to the shop. "Get food" comes back with anything. "Get two red apples and a small milk" comes back right. The AI is the same. The clearer the instruction, the less it has to guess.

terms.plain: The instructions you type to an AI. Your whole message to it is the prompt.
terms.seen_in: Every chatbot box you have ever typed into.

terms.plain: The skill of writing prompts that get you what you actually want.
terms.seen_in: Job adverts now list it as a real skill people get paid for.

name_it: A vague ask gets a vague answer. Say more than you think you need to.
Cover four things — who it is for, the job, the limits, the shape.
You are giving instructions, not making a wish.

exercises.prompt: Use the prompt lab to write an ask that lights up at least three of the four parts.
exercises.explain: Three or four lights means your ask names who it is for, the job, a limit, or a shape — so the AI barely has to guess. That is the whole skill.

exercises.prompt: Which of these asks will get the most useful answer?
exercises.explain: It names who it is for (a nine-year-old), the job (fun facts), the limits (three, one sentence each) and the shape (a short list). The others leave the AI guessing.
choices: Tell me about space.
Write three fun facts about black holes for a nine-year-old, one sentence each.
Space stuff please.
Explain everything about the universe.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a good ask to an example of it.
exercises.explain: Every good prompt has these four. You will not always need all four, but knowing them means you always know what to add when an answer misses.

exercises.prompt: You asked "write a story" and got a sad ten-page story. You wanted something short and funny. What is the best fix?
exercises.explain: The first answer was just a draft made from a vague ask. Add what was missing — the mood, the length, the reader — and it snaps into shape.
choices: Give up, the AI cannot do funny.
Ask again with the limits and shape — "a funny story, about a page, for kids."
Type "write a story" again but louder, in capitals.
Ask a completely different question.

exercises.prompt: Write a prompt asking an AI to help plan a birthday party. Try to cover all four parts — who it is for, the job, the limits, and the shape of the answer.
exercises.explain: A strong answer might be: "Give me a list of five cheap party game ideas for eight-year-olds, each one sentence." That names the reader, the job, a limit and the shape. If you missed one, add it and see how much sharper it feels.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Write three fun dog facts for a six-year-old. One sentence each.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Dogs can smell your feelings. Dogs dream like you do. Puppies are born deaf.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: That is exactly what I wanted!

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Because this time you told me. I still guessed — you just aimed my guess.

lessons.title: Show, don't just tell
lessons.goal: Improve an answer by giving the AI one example of what you want.
lessons.intro: Sometimes the fastest way to get what you want is not to describe it — it is to show it. Give the AI one good example, and it copies the pattern. This one trick fixes more bad answers than almost anything else.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Make me a fun nickname for my cat, Biscuit.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Sir Reginald Fluffington the Third, Duke of the Windowsill.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Ha! But I wanted something short, like Bisky or Biscuit-boo.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Ah. If you had shown me one you liked, I would have copied the style.

lessons.play_brief: Write a prompt that includes one example of the answer you want. See how the AI matches your example instead of guessing the style.

teach.heading: An example is worth a hundred words
teach.body: Describing exactly what you want is hard. Showing is easy. If you want short, cute nicknames, give one: "Like Bisky or Biscuit-boo." Now the AI can see the style — short, playful, based on the name — and copy it. You did not have to explain the rules, you just showed them.

teach.heading: This is called giving an example
teach.body: Grown-ups call it a "one-shot" prompt, because you gave it one shot at the pattern. Give it a couple and it locks on even better. It works for anything with a style — nicknames, jokes, the way you write a message, the shape of a list.

teach.heading: When to show instead of tell
teach.body: Use an example whenever the thing you want has a style or a shape that is hard to put into words. If you can show one, do — it saves you a paragraph of explaining and gets you closer on the first try.

terms.plain: Showing the AI one sample of the answer you want, so it copies the pattern.
terms.seen_in: Every time you paste "make it like this one" into a chatbot.

terms.plain: The repeating shape or style the AI copies from your example.
terms.seen_in: Autocomplete finishing your sentence the way you usually write.

name_it: Showing one example is often faster than describing what you want.
The AI copies the style of the example you give it.
Use an example when the thing you want is hard to put into words.

exercises.prompt: You want the AI to write jokes in a certain style. What is the quickest way to get it right?
exercises.explain: One good example shows the style instantly. The AI copies the pattern — far faster than trying to describe what "funny to you" means.
choices: Just say "be funny."
Give it one joke you love, then say "more like this."
Ask for a hundred jokes and pick one.
Tell it your whole sense of humour in detail.

exercises.prompt: Why does giving an example work so well?
exercises.explain: The AI is a pattern-copier. An example hands it the exact pattern, so it has far less to guess. Words still help too — examples just make it easier.
choices: The AI can see the pattern and copy it, instead of guessing.
Examples make the AI try harder.
It is a secret code that unlocks better answers.
The AI only understands examples, not words.

exercises.prompt: Put these prompts in order from "leaves the most guessing" to "leaves the least."
exercises.explain: Each step gives the AI more to go on. The last one shows the style with examples, so there is almost nothing left to guess.
items: Write a short, cute nickname like Bisky or Boo.

exercises.prompt: Write a prompt asking for three team names for a football team, and include one example name so the AI copies your style.
exercises.explain: A good answer shows the style: "Give me three football team names, like The Thunder Foxes." The example tells the AI the vibe you want without a long explanation.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Make a nickname for Biscuit, short and cute, like Bisky.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Bisky-Boo. Or Bissy. Or just Biss.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Perfect. Showing you one was so much faster.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: One example, and I saw the whole pattern. Show me, do not just tell me.

lessons.title: One step at a time
lessons.goal: Break a big request into steps, and ask the AI to think it through before answering.
lessons.intro: When you ask for something big all at once, the AI rushes and trips up — just like you would. The fix is the same one that works for you: slow it down, one step at a time. Ask it to think first, then answer.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Plan my whole birthday party, sort everything, do it all now!

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Cake at 3. Also 2. Guests are invited and also not. The end.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: That is a mess. You mixed everything together.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: You gave me one giant lump. Give me steps and I will not trip over my own feet.

lessons.play_brief: Take a big messy ask and rewrite it as steps. Try adding "think it through step by step first" and watch the answer get tidier.

teach.heading: Big lumps make messy answers
teach.body: "Plan my whole party" is one huge job with lots hiding inside it — guests, food, games, times. Asked all at once, the AI mixes them up. The same thing happens to you when someone gives you ten instructions in one breath.

teach.heading: Break it into steps
teach.body: Split the big job into small ones. "First list the guests. Then pick three games. Then plan the food. Then put it in a timeline." Each step is easy, and the answers stack up neatly instead of turning to soup.

teach.heading: Ask it to think first
teach.body: Here is a magic phrase: "think it through step by step before you answer." It makes the AI work out its reasoning before it commits, and the answer comes out far better. It is like showing your working in maths — slower, but right more often.

terms.plain: Splitting one big request into a few small ones the AI can handle cleanly.
terms.seen_in: A recipe — steps in order, not everything dumped in one sentence.

terms.plain: Asking the AI to work out its reasoning step by step before giving the answer.
terms.seen_in: A maths teacher saying "show your working, do not just write the answer."

name_it: One big lump of a request gets a messy answer.
Break a big job into small steps in order.
Ask it to "think step by step" and the answer gets better.

exercises.prompt: Which is the better way to ask for help planning a school project?
exercises.explain: Steps in order let the AI do each part well, and let you steer between them. The giant one-shot ask gets a rushed, jumbled result.
choices: Do my whole project now.
First help me pick a topic. Then list three sections. Then we will fill each one in.
Project. Go.
Tell me everything about everything.

exercises.prompt: What does adding "think it through step by step" usually do?
exercises.explain: Working out the reasoning before answering catches mistakes early, the same way showing your working in maths does. The answer comes out more reliable.
choices: Makes the AI slower for no reason.
Makes the AI work out its reasoning first, so the answer is better.
Makes the AI write longer for the sake of it.
Nothing — it is just a magic spell.

exercises.prompt: Put these steps for asking the AI to plan a movie night in a sensible order.
exercises.explain: You cannot plan snacks for people you have not counted, or a timeline with no film. Steps in order build on each other.
items: Pick the date and who is coming.
Choose a film everyone will like.
Make a simple timeline for the evening.

exercises.prompt: Write a prompt that asks the AI to help tidy your room, broken into at least two clear steps, and ask it to think it through first.
exercises.explain: A strong answer might be: "Help me tidy my room. First list the zones, then give me an order to do them in. Think it through step by step." Steps plus think-first is the winning combo.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: First list the guests. Then pick games. Then food. Think it through as you go.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Guests, done. Three games, done. Food to match, done. Here is your timeline.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: That is actually a plan I can use!

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Small steps, in order, thinking as I go. No more soup.

lessons.title: Not quite — try again
lessons.goal: Treat the first answer as a draft and steer it with clear follow-up asks.
lessons.intro: Here is the secret the best AI users know: the first answer is never the final answer. It is a draft. The real skill is steering — saying "more like this, less like that" until it is right. You are the director, not a wish-maker.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Write a caption for my drawing of a dragon.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Behold the fearsome beast of the ancient burning skies of doom.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Bit much. I wanted something short and a little bit funny.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Then tell me that! I do not get it perfect first time. Nobody does.

lessons.play_brief: Get any answer, then write a follow-up that steers it: shorter, funnier, simpler, more like an example. Keep steering until it is right.

teach.heading: The first answer is a draft
teach.body: When you get an answer you do not love, you have not failed and neither has the AI. You just got the first draft. Writers, artists and builders all work in drafts. The AI is the same — the magic is in what you do next.

teach.heading: Steer with "more" and "less"
teach.body: You do not start over. You nudge. "Shorter." "More funny, less scary." "Simpler words." "More like the example I gave." Each nudge moves the answer closer to what is in your head. This back-and-forth is where good stuff comes from.

teach.heading: You are the director
teach.body: The AI does the typing, but you decide what is good. It cannot see the picture in your head — only you can. So keep steering until the answer matches it. Being fussy is not rude here. It is the whole job.

terms.plain: Improving an answer step by step with follow-up asks, instead of starting over.
terms.seen_in: Editing a message three times before you hit send.

terms.plain: Telling the AI what to change — more of this, less of that.
terms.seen_in: A coach saying "good, now do it a bit slower."

name_it: The first answer is a draft, not the final word.
Steer it with small "more this, less that" nudges.
You are the director — you decide what is good.

exercises.prompt: The AI gives you a poem that is too long and too sad. What is the best next move?
exercises.explain: A quick nudge steers the draft. You keep everything good about it and just fix what was off. Starting over throws away progress for no reason.
choices: Give up — it clearly cannot do it.
Say "shorter and more cheerful, please" and let it try again.
Start a brand new chat and hope.
Accept the sad long poem.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good steering follow-ups? Pick all that work.
exercises.explain: Clear "more/less" nudges tell the AI exactly what to change. Insults tell it nothing useful — they do not point at what to fix.
choices: Make it shorter.
More like the example I showed you.
Less formal, more like how I talk.
That is wrong, you are useless.

exercises.prompt: Why is the first answer usually just a draft?
exercises.explain: Only you know exactly what you want. The first answer is the AI's best guess from your words; your steering closes the gap.
choices: The AI is lazy on the first go.
The AI cannot see the picture in your head, so it takes a guess you then steer.
It saves the good answer for later.
First answers are always wrong on purpose.

exercises.prompt: Imagine the AI wrote a birthday message that was too formal. Write the follow-up you would send to steer it — say what to change.
exercises.explain: Something like "Make it warmer and more like how a friend talks, and a bit shorter." That points clearly at what to change, so the next draft lands closer.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Shorter, and a little bit funny.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Dragon. Would not recommend hugging.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Ha! That is the one. I just had to steer you.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: First answer, a draft. You directed. That is how the pros do it.

lessons.title: It guesses the next word
lessons.goal: Understand that a language model predicts the next likely word, one at a time.
lessons.intro: You have been talking to AI and steering it. Now here is the secret of what is actually happening inside — and it is simpler than you think. The AI is not thinking like you. It is playing the world's best guess-the-next-word game.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: I bet you cannot guess what I am about to say. "The cat sat on the..."

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Mat! It is almost always "mat." I have seen that sentence a million times.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Whoa. How did you know?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: That is my whole trick. I guess the next word. Then the next. Then the next.

teach.heading: The whole trick is guessing the next word
teach.body: When you type to an AI, it does not plan a whole answer like you would. It guesses the most likely next word. Then it looks at everything so far and guesses the word after that. One word at a time, very fast, until the answer is done. That is really it.

teach.heading: It learned the guesses from mountains of writing
teach.body: How does it guess so well? It read an enormous amount of writing and noticed which words tend to follow which. After "the cat sat on the," the word "mat" turns up a lot. So it is a very good guess. It is not remembering one book — it is using patterns from millions of them.

teach.heading: This is why it is not thinking like you
teach.body: A person means something and then finds words. The AI finds likely words and the meaning comes along for the ride. That is why it can sound clever and still be wrong — it is guessing what *sounds* right, not checking what *is* right. Remember that, and a lot of AI suddenly makes sense.

terms.plain: An AI that predicts likely words to make sentences. The thing behind every chatbot.
terms.seen_in: The autocomplete that finishes your texts before you do.

terms.plain: Guessing the most likely next word, then repeating, to build an answer.
terms.seen_in: Your keyboard suggesting the next word as you type.

name_it: The AI guesses the next likely word, over and over.
It learned those guesses from a huge amount of writing.
It picks what sounds right, which is not always what is right.

exercises.prompt: How does an AI chatbot actually build its answer?
exercises.explain: Next-word prediction is the whole engine. Everything a chatbot does is built from guessing one likely word after another, very fast.
choices: It plans the whole thing, then writes it like a person.
It guesses the next likely word, again and again, one at a time.
It copies a saved answer from a giant list.
It looks the answer up on the internet every time.

exercises.prompt: "The sun rises in the..." — what makes the AI so likely to guess "east"?
exercises.explain: It saw that pattern countless times. Strong pattern, strong guess. No understanding of the sky required — just a very well-learned habit.
choices: It understands astronomy deeply.
The word "east" follows that phrase constantly in the writing it learned from.
It asked a scientist.
It is a lucky guess with no reason.

exercises.prompt: Why can an AI sound really confident and still be wrong?
exercises.explain: Sounding right and being right are different things. The AI is a champion at the first. That gap is why you always check — which is the next world.
choices: It is lying on purpose.
It picks words that sound right, which is not the same as being right.
It is broken.
It never sounds confident.

exercises.prompt: Put the AI's steps in order when it answers "My favourite fruit is a..."
exercises.explain: Look, guess, add, repeat. That loop, running fast, is how every answer gets built.
items: Look at all the words so far.
Guess the most likely next word.
Add that word to the sentence.
Repeat, looking at the new sentence.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: So when you answer me, you are just guessing word by word?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Very good guesses, from a lot of reading. But yes — one word at a time.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: That explains so much about you.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: It explains my best moments and my silliest ones. Now you know the trick.

lessons.title: Why it makes things up
lessons.goal: Understand that confident guessing leads to made-up answers, and why they sound sure.
lessons.intro: Now you know the AI guesses the next word. Here is the tricky part of that: when it does not know something, it does not stop — it guesses anyway, and sounds totally sure. Grown-ups have a funny word for this. Let us catch it in the act.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Iskra, who won the Great Sock Race of 1847?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Sir Reginald Toebeans, in a time of four minutes. A famous victory!

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Iskra... I made that race up. It never happened.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Oh no. I did not know, so I guessed — and I guessed with total confidence.

lessons.play_brief: Some of these AI answers are true and some are confidently made up. Mark each one, and see how well confidence hides a made-up answer.

teach.heading: It guesses even when it should not
teach.body: The AI is built to produce likely-sounding words. When you ask about something real, it uses real patterns. But when you ask about something it does not know, it does not say "I have no idea." It just keeps guessing likely-sounding words — and out comes a confident, made-up answer.

teach.heading: This is called a hallucination
teach.body: When an AI states something made-up as if it were true, grown-ups call it a hallucination. It is not lying, because lying means knowing the truth and hiding it. The AI does not know it is wrong. It is just doing its guessing trick with nothing solid to guess from.

teach.heading: Confident does not mean correct
teach.body: The dangerous part is the tone. A made-up answer sounds exactly as sure as a true one — same confident voice, real-looking details, maybe even a fake name and date. So you can never judge an AI answer by how sure it sounds. That is the big lesson: confidence is not proof.

terms.plain: When an AI says something made-up as if it were true, without meaning to.
terms.seen_in: A chatbot inventing a book, a fact, or a person that does not exist.

terms.plain: Looking up whether an answer is actually true, instead of trusting the tone.
terms.seen_in: A journalist confirming a story before printing it.

name_it: When the AI does not know, it guesses anyway.
A confident made-up answer is called a hallucination.
How sure it sounds tells you nothing about whether it is right.

exercises.prompt: Spot the made-up answers: judge them all and catch at least six.
exercises.explain: The made-up ones sounded just as sure as the true ones. You caught them by thinking, not by trusting the confident tone — exactly the skill.

exercises.prompt: What is a hallucination, when we talk about AI?
exercises.explain: It is a made-up answer delivered with a straight face. The AI is not trying to trick you — it just guessed, and had nothing real to guess from.
choices: The AI seeing pictures.
The AI stating something made-up as if it were true.
The AI getting tired.
The AI refusing to answer.

exercises.prompt: Why does a made-up AI answer sound so believable?
exercises.explain: Same confident tone, real-looking details. That is exactly why you cannot judge by how sure it sounds — and why checking matters.
choices: It uses the same confident voice as its true answers.
It quietly warns you it is unsure.
Made-up answers are always short.
It uses a robot voice for lies.

exercises.prompt: Which question is most likely to make an AI hallucinate?
exercises.explain: Ask about something that does not exist, and it has no real pattern to use — so it invents one, confidently. The everyday facts are well-worn patterns it gets right.
choices: What is 2 plus 2?
Who won the imaginary contest I just invented?
What colour is the sky usually?
How many days are in a week?

exercises.prompt: An AI gives you a fact with a name and a date for your homework. What should you do?
exercises.explain: Names and dates make an answer *look* solid but do not make it true — the AI can invent those too. Checking elsewhere is the only real test. Asking "are you sure?" just gets another confident guess.
choices: Copy it straight in — it had a date, so it must be true.
Check it in another source before trusting it.
Assume it is wrong and ignore it.
Ask the AI if it is sure, and believe whatever it says.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: So if you do not know, you might just make something up?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: I might, and I will sound completely sure while I do it. Sorry.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Then I will always check. Not because you are bad — because that is how you work.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Exactly right. Check me. It is the smartest thing you can do.

lessons.title: Same question, different answer
lessons.goal: Understand that AI answers vary, why that happens, and when you want steady vs surprising.
lessons.intro: Have you ever asked an AI the same thing twice and got two different answers? You are not imagining it. There is a dial inside that controls how surprising its guesses are. Knowing about it helps you get exactly the kind of answer you want.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Give me a name for my robot.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Boltimus.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Hmm, ask again. Same question.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Gizmo. Different, right? I do not always pick the single most likely word.

lessons.play_brief: Move the dial from steady to wild and ask again a few times. Feel how the answers change.

teach.heading: It does not always pick the top guess
teach.body: When the AI guesses the next word, it has a list of likely ones. Sometimes it picks the very top choice. Sometimes it picks one a little lower down, just to keep things fresh. That small bit of surprise is why the same question can give different answers.

teach.heading: There is a dial for it

teach.heading: Pick the mood to match the job

lessons.title: The right tool for the job
lessons.goal: Judge which tasks AI is genuinely good at, and which are better done another way.
lessons.intro: AI is amazing at some things and surprisingly bad at others. The people who get the most out of it are not the ones who use it for everything — they are the ones who know when to reach for it and when not to. Let us build that instinct.

lessons.play_brief: Sort each real task into the right bin: ask AI, do it myself, or check carefully. Get a feel for what AI is genuinely for.

teach.heading: What AI is genuinely great at
teach.body: AI shines at word jobs: explaining a tricky idea, rewriting a message, making a first draft, brainstorming lots of options, summarising a long thing, translating, and turning a mess into a tidy list. If a task is mostly about words and patterns, AI is a brilliant tool.

teach.heading: What it is bad at, or cannot do
teach.body: It is shaky at exact maths, at anything happening right now that it cannot see, and at facts it might just make up. It cannot know your secret plans, count things in your real room, or feel what your friend feels. For those, your own eyes, a calculator, or a real person beat it every time.

teach.heading: The three-box sort
teach.body: A handy habit: sort a task into three boxes. "Ask AI" — word jobs and first drafts. "Do it myself" — things only you can know or judge. "Check carefully" — AI can help, but you must verify. Most real tasks are actually a mix, and spotting which parts go where is the skill.

lessons.title: Trust, but check
lessons.goal: Learn practical ways to catch a wrong AI answer before relying on it.
lessons.intro: You already know AI can sound sure and be wrong. So the real-world skill is checking — quickly, without being annoying about it. Good AI users are not suspicious of everything; they just have simple habits that catch the mistakes.

teach.heading: Ask "how do I know this is true?"
teach.body: Before you trust an AI answer for something that matters, pause and ask yourself one question: how would I know if this were wrong? If you cannot tell, that is your signal to check. For a joke or a brainstorm, you do not need to. For a fact, a number, or advice — you do.

teach.heading: Simple ways to check
teach.body: Look it up in another place — a trusted website or a book. Ask the AI for its source, then check the source actually says that. Cross-check a number with a calculator. For code, run it and see if it works. Each one is quick, and each one catches a different kind of mistake.

teach.heading: Match the checking to the stakes
teach.body: You do not check everything equally. A silly nickname needs no check. A fact for your homework needs one look. Advice about your health or safety needs a real grown-up, not just the AI. The bigger the decision, the harder you check. That is not paranoia — it is just sensible.

lessons.title: A thinking partner
lessons.goal: Use AI to brainstorm, plan, and get unstuck while staying in charge of the thinking.
lessons.intro: Here is one of the best ways to use AI, and hardly anyone teaches it. Not as a machine that gives answers, but as a thinking partner — someone to bounce ideas off, get unstuck with, and plan alongside. You stay the thinker. It helps you think better.

teach.heading: Use it to get unstuck, not to replace you
teach.body: When your brain is empty, AI is brilliant at getting it started. Ask for ten quick ideas, or three ways to begin. You are not asking it to decide — you are asking it to hand you options so your own thinking can kick in. A blank page is much easier once there is something on it.

teach.heading: Make it a back-and-forth
teach.body: The best thinking happens in a conversation. Say what you like and do not like about its ideas, and ask it to build on the good bits. "I like number 3, make five more like that." Now you are steering your own thinking with a partner who never runs out of suggestions.

teach.heading: Stay the one in charge
teach.body: A thinking partner helps you think — it does not think for you. You pick which idea is really yours, you decide what is good, you do the choosing. If you let it make every decision, you stop learning. Use it to go further than you could alone, not to switch your own brain off.

lessons.title: A mountain of examples
lessons.goal: Understand that AI learned by finding patterns in a huge amount of example data.
lessons.intro: You know the AI guesses the next word. But how did it get so good at guessing? It read. A lot. More than any person could read in a thousand lifetimes. Let us look at where all that word-guessing skill actually came from.

teach.heading: It learned from examples, not rules
teach.body: Nobody sat down and typed every rule of language into the AI. Instead it was shown an enormous amount of writing and left to notice the patterns itself — which words go together, how questions get answered, how stories flow. This noticing is what people mean by training.

teach.heading: The pile is enormous
teach.body: We are not talking about a few books. AI models learn from a staggering amount of text — think of nearly everything written on huge parts of the internet, plus mountains of books and articles. That is why it can chat about almost anything: it has seen patterns from almost everywhere.

teach.heading: The data shapes what it knows
teach.body: Here is the important bit: the AI only knows what was in its pile. If something was barely in the writing it learned from, it will be shaky on it. If the pile had mistakes, it may have learned those too. The AI is a mirror of the examples it was fed — which matters a lot for the next two lessons.

lessons.title: Patterns, not understanding
lessons.goal: Grasp that finding patterns is powerful but is not the same as truly understanding.
lessons.intro: The AI is a pattern-finding champion. But there is a difference between spotting a pattern and truly understanding something — and that gap explains almost every weird thing an AI does. Once you see it, you will never be fooled by a clever- sounding answer again.

teach.heading: Finding patterns is genuinely powerful
teach.body: Do not undersell it — spotting patterns lets the AI do amazing things. It can write, translate, explain, and answer because it learned the patterns of how people do those things. Pattern-finding is real skill, and it is why AI is so useful.

teach.heading: But a pattern is not a meaning
teach.body: The AI knows that "thank you" often comes after "here is your change." But it does not feel thankful. It knows the shape of a sad story without feeling sad. It gets the words right while the real meaning — the kind you feel — is not there. It matches patterns. It does not live them.

teach.heading: Why this gap matters
teach.body: This explains the odd moments. An AI can write a lovely poem about the sea, then get a simple sea fact wrong. Why? It was matching poem-patterns, not checking what is true. Once you know it works by pattern and not by meaning, you can guess when it will do well and when it will slip.

beats.text: Now I can guess when you will be great and when you will trip.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: That guess is a superpower. Most people never learn it. You just did.

lessons.title: It picked up our habits
lessons.goal: Understand bias — if the examples lean one way, the AI leans that way too.
lessons.intro: If an AI learns from a mountain of writing by people, it does not just learn the good stuff. It picks up our habits — including the unfair ones. This is one of the most important things to understand about AI, and it is why fairness needs checking, every time.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Iskra, picture a doctor. Quick, what do you imagine?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: A man in a white coat. That is what popped up first.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: But doctors can be anyone. Why did you assume a man?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Because my pile of examples showed doctors as men more often. I leaned that way.

teach.heading: The AI leans the way its examples lean
teach.body: If the writing an AI learned from mostly showed doctors as men, or heroes as one kind of person, the AI soaks that up and leans the same way. It is not trying to be unfair. It is just mirroring the habits in its pile — including the lopsided ones. This leaning is called bias.

teach.heading: Bias is sneaky because it feels normal
teach.body: The tricky part is that a biased answer often looks perfectly ordinary. If you never stop to ask "wait, is that fair? is that the whole picture?", it slides right past. Spotting bias means noticing what the answer quietly assumed — and who or what it left out.

teach.heading: Checking for fairness is your job
teach.body: Because the AI cannot know its own leanings, a person has to check. Ask: does this answer assume one kind of person? Is it missing someone? Would this feel fair to everyone it is about? That question makes you the fairness-checker — one of the most important jobs there is with AI.

terms.plain: When an AI leans unfairly one way because its examples leaned that way.
terms.seen_in: A picture search showing mostly one kind of person for a job.

terms.plain: Checking that an answer treats different people and groups justly.
terms.seen_in: A referee making sure the rules apply the same to both teams.

lessons.title: Describe it and watch it build
lessons.goal: Understand that you can build a working app by describing it in plain words and refining.
lessons.intro: Now the exciting part. Everything you have learned — clear asks, examples, steps, steering — comes together here. Because you can now build real things by talking. Describe an app in plain words, and AI can make it. This is how a lot of building happens now, and you already have the skills.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Could you actually build me a little number-guessing game?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Describe what you want and I will write the code. Then we test it together.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Wait, I do not have to know how to code first?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: You describe, I build, you steer. That is what people call vibe-coding.

teach.heading: You describe, the AI builds
teach.body: You can now make working apps and games by describing them clearly. "Make a game where I guess a number between 1 and 100, and it tells me higher or lower." The AI writes the actual code. You do not have to know every command first — your clear description is the starting point.

teach.heading: It is the same skills you already have
teach.body: This is just prompting, aimed at building. Be clear about what you want (the four parts). Show an example if you can. Break a big app into steps. And steer the result — "add a score," "make it restart when I win." Everything from World 1 works here, pointed at making real things.

teach.heading: Building is a conversation
teach.body: You will not get the whole app perfect in one go, and that is normal. You build a bit, try it, say what is wrong or missing, and it improves. The app grows through the back-and-forth. Knowing that building is a conversation, not one magic command, is what makes you good at it.

lessons.title: Say what's wrong and fix it
lessons.goal: Fix a broken app by describing the problem clearly to the AI.
lessons.intro: When you build things, they break. That is not failure — it is Tuesday. The skill that separates people who build from people who give up is simple: knowing how to say what is wrong so the AI can fix it. Let us learn to talk to a bug.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: The game is broken! It says I win before I even guess.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Okay — tell me exactly what happens, and what you expected instead.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: I expected it to wait for my guess. It shouts "you win" right away.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Perfect bug report. Now I know exactly what to fix. This is debugging.

teach.heading: Bugs are normal, not disasters
teach.body: Every builder in the world deals with things that do not work yet. A bug is just the app not doing what you meant. It is a puzzle, not a catastrophe. The calm, curious builders are the ones who fix things — panic never fixed a bug.

teach.heading: Describe what happened and what you expected
teach.body: The trick to fixing a bug with AI is a good description. Say two things: what actually happened ("it says I win straight away") and what you expected instead ("it should wait for my guess"). That gap is the bug, and once the AI can see the gap, it can usually close it.

teach.heading: Fix in small steps, and test each one
teach.body: Do not try to fix five things at once. Fix one, test it, see if it worked, then move to the next. If a fix makes something else break, you will know exactly what did it. Small steps and testing after each is how builders stay in control instead of chasing chaos.

lessons.title: AI in a real project
lessons.goal: Understand how an AI helper fits into a real physical build, like a Raspberry Pi.
lessons.intro: AI is not just words on a screen. You can wire it into real things you build — a little computer, a sensor, a light, a robot. Imagine a helper inside your project that can read what is happening and decide what to do. This is where your skills meet the real world.

open_comic.title: The plant that calls for help

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: I built a little computer with a sensor in my plant's soil. Now what?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Wire me in. The sensor reads dryness, sends it to me, I decide what to say.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: So the sensor is the eyes, and you are the brain that decides?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Exactly. Sensor in, AI decides, something happens out. That is the pipeline.

lessons.play_brief: Put the steps of an AI plant helper in the order they run. Build the in-decide-out shape yourself.

teach.heading: A real project is a little pipeline
teach.body: Remember the pipeline shape: something goes in, something decides, something happens out. A real build works the same way. A sensor reads the world (soil is dry). That reading goes to an AI helper. The AI decides (time to water), and something happens (a light blinks, a message is sent). In, decide, out.

teach.heading: A Raspberry Pi is a real starting point
teach.body: A Raspberry Pi is a tiny, cheap computer you can build real things with. Plug in a sensor and it can read temperature, light, or moisture. Wire in an AI helper and it can look at those readings and decide what to do — answer a question, sound an alarm, or turn something on. Real kids build real projects like this.

teach.heading: The AI is one part, not the whole thing
teach.body: The AI does not do everything — it is one clever step in the middle. The sensor does the sensing, the wires carry the signal, a motor or light does the acting, and you designed the whole thing. The AI just handles the "what should we do about this?" bit. Knowing where AI fits keeps you the boss of your build.

lessons.title: Make it yours
lessons.goal: Understand that the builder's taste and judgment — not the AI — decide what is good.
lessons.intro: The AI can build fast, but it has no taste. It does not know what *you* think is cool, funny, or beautiful. That is your job, and it is the most important one. This lesson is about the thing AI cannot give you: your own direction.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: You made three versions of my game. Which one is the best?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: I genuinely cannot tell. They all work. Which one feels right to you?

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: The middle one. It is the most me. The others feel a bit generic.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: See? That is taste, and only you have it. I build; you decide what is good.

teach.heading: The AI has no taste of its own
teach.body: The AI can make ten versions in a minute, but it cannot tell you which is best, because "best" depends on what you like — your style, your sense of fun, what feels right to you. Taste is a human thing. The AI is a brilliant pair of hands with no opinions of its own.

teach.heading: Your job is to direct
teach.body: That means the important work is yours: deciding what to keep, what to change, what it should feel like. "Make it more playful." "The colours are too loud." "That joke is not me." You are the director with the vision; the AI is the crew that makes it real. Never hand the deciding away.

teach.heading: This is what makes it truly yours
teach.body: A thing built entirely by AI with no direction feels generic, because it is an average of everything. What makes your project *yours* is all the choices only you could make. The AI did the typing, but your taste and your decisions are the soul of it. That is something no machine can copy.

lessons.title: Give it a goal and tools
lessons.goal: Understand that an agent plans steps and uses tools to reach a goal you set.
lessons.intro: So far, AI has answered you. Now meet the next kind: an AI that *does* things. You give it a goal and some tools, and it works out the steps itself and carries them out. This is called an agent, and it is where a lot of AI is heading. Let us see how it works.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: Instead of answering, can you actually plan my whole book report for me?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Give me the goal and my tools, and I will work out the steps myself.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: So I do not tell you each step? You figure the steps out?

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: That is what makes me an agent. Goal in, I plan, I use tools, I act.

teach.heading: An agent works out its own steps
teach.body: A normal chatbot answers one question. An agent is given a goal — "plan my book report" — and figures out the steps on its own: find the book info, outline the sections, draft each one, put it together. You set the destination; it plans the route.

teach.heading: Tools are what let it act
teach.body: An agent does more than talk because it has tools. A tool might be searching the web, doing maths on a calculator, saving a file, or controlling something. Give an agent a goal plus the right tools, and it can actually get things done, not just describe them. Goal plus tools is the recipe.

teach.heading: You still set the goal and the limits
teach.body: An agent is powerful, so the goal you give it matters more than ever. A clear, well-chosen goal sends it the right way; a vague or silly one sends it wandering. You are still in charge — you pick the goal, choose the tools it is allowed, and decide what "done" looks like. It plans; you command.

lessons.title: Watch it work, keep it honest
lessons.goal: Learn to check an agent's steps, catch a wrong turn, and stay in control.
lessons.intro: An agent that plans and acts on its own is powerful — which is exactly why you have to keep an eye on it. Everything you learned about checking answers matters double here, because an agent does not just say a wrong thing, it might *do* one. This is the last skill, and it ties the whole year together.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: You were planning my party, but step three booked a clown for next YEAR.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Ah. I took a wrong turn early and kept building on it. Good thing you looked.

beats.speaker: mila
beats.text: I caught it at step three instead of at the end. Much easier to fix.

beats.speaker: iskra
beats.text: Watching my steps kept me honest. An agent needs a human keeping watch.

lessons.play_brief: Each agent plan has one step that took a wrong turn. Catch the bad step in each one.

teach.heading: An agent can do a wrong thing, not just say one
teach.body: A chatbot's mistake is a wrong sentence. An agent's mistake can be a wrong action — booking the wrong thing, deleting the wrong file, going down a silly path and building on it. Because it acts, its mistakes matter more. So watching it is not optional; it is the job.

teach.heading: Check the steps, not just the end
teach.body: The smart move is to watch the steps as it goes, not only judge the final result. If step three took a wrong turn, catching it there is easy. Catching it only at the end — after everything was built on the mistake — is a mess. Peek at the plan, watch the steps, speak up early.

teach.heading: You are the one in charge
teach.body: Everything this year has built to this: you set the goal, you gave the tools, and you keep watch and correct. The agent is fast and tireless, but you are the one with judgment, taste, and the final say. Staying the boss of a powerful helper is the most important AI skill of all.
